extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general readers of American government and politics
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook exposition of how the U.S. Congress conducts daily business (committee selection, bill introduction and floor procedure, minority privileges, investigations) and how the federal judiciary is organized and operates (Supreme Court, courts of appeals, district courts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules committee composition and selection (1910 resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules committee should consist of ten members instead of five, that the said committee should be elected by the House instead of appointed by the Speaker, and that the Speaker himself should no longer be a member of the committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes the 1910/1911 change (Democrats victorious in 1910 provided that all committees should be elected by the House). Also explains this change was likely more nominal than real because selections were still made in caucuses; it reduced the Speaker's prestige and shifted practical power to other party leaders (notably the chairman of the ways and means committee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee selection still conducted in party caucuses
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection [of committees] is still made in caucuses as before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although committees are formally elected by the House, party caucuses effectively determine selections; therefore formal rules changes may have limited practical effect on who actually controls committee membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: House leadership distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: For the present, the leadership is vested in the chairman of the ways and means committee aided by the Speaker and the chairmen of certain of the other more important committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains practical distribution of leadership power in the House and notes continuing complaints from minority members about 'tyranny' and 'dictation' despite diffusion of formal powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening procedures of a new Congress (House)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the opening of a new Congress the House is called to order by the clerk of the last House, who calls the roll and, finding a quorum present, announces that they are ready for nominations for Speaker; after the nominee is ratified he takes the oath administered by the member longest in continuous service; other officers are chosen and the President of the Senate and the House are informed that the House is ready for business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also includes adoption of rules of the preceding Congress (usually carried despite minority protests) and reading/approval of names of committeemen selected by caucuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate opening procedures and continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate is a continuous body: at each new Congress only one-third of the members are renewed; the Vice-President takes the chair or a president pro tempore in his absence; newly elected Senators are called in alphabetical order and take the oath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes informational notifications to the President and House and how both houses become ready for business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of introducing bills in the House
rubrics_metrics.description: Any member may introduce any measure by drafting it and depositing it on the clerk's table, or may introduce a petition for a bill to be referred to a committee for drafting; important bills are usually drafted by majority members of the committee in charge of the subject-matter; committees sometimes cooperate with Senate committees, the President, or party leaders may be consulted, and a caucus may be held even before introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that while any member may introduce legislation, really important measures are typically prepared by committees and party leaders; consultation and pre-introduction caucuses are common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee referral and committee actions on public bills
rubrics_metrics.description: On introduction all public bills are referred by the Speaker to the appropriate committee which may hold hearings and give the matter any amount of attention it sees fit; the committee may report the bill favorably unamended, amend it and report it in such form, report unfavorably, or neglect it altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes variety of possible committee dispositions (including neglect) and that important committees may report at any time from the floor while other committees leave reports on the clerk's table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement on calendar and debate scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless it is a highly privileged matter, a bill when reported is placed on a calendar for debate according to the rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that placement on the calendar governs when a bill is reached for debate and that different classes of measures have different scheduling treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee of the Whole for revenue and appropriation bills
rubrics_metrics.description: All public bills raising revenue or authorizing the appropriation of money or property are considered in the committee of the whole House; in this form one hundred constitute a quorum and the Speaker resigns the chair to some other member; stages are 'general debate, reading for amendment under the five-minute rule; order to lay aside with a favorable recommendation, or to rise and report; reporting to the House.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the procedural stages of the committee of the whole and the lower quorum requirement (100) compared to full House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second and third readings and amendment procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills not required to be considered in the committee of the whole are read a second time when reached on the calendar and are then open to discussion and amendment in the House; the third reading usually takes place by title and the question is put by the Speaker as a matter of course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the ordinary floor progression of bills and the practical limitation on substantive debate at third reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional minority privileges in Congress (roll call, quorum, unanimous consent)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the request of one-fifth of the members present, the roll of the House must be called on any question and the yeas and nays entered on the journal; no business shall be done unless a quorum is present, and the minority may frequently raise the question of a quorum; much legislative business is done under the rule of unanimous consent, which the minority may refuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how these provisions give the minority tactical means to block or delay proceedings and to force the majority to adopt certain policies; example: minority threats to refuse unanimous consent and to call for yeas and nays until demands are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minority obstructive tactics and leverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The minority may refuse unanimous consent to legislation, call for yeas and nays on every affirmative proposition, or otherwise exercise privileges under the rules for the purpose of obstructing business until the majority agrees to report on certain bills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives historical example (March 1903) of such a minority strategy to compel consideration of specific reform measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission and final enactment formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: When a bill has passed either house it is transmitted to the other body by the secretary who announces that the Senate has passed bill No. X and requests concurrence; if the other house passes it, the measure is signed by the President of the Senate and the Speaker and sent to the President of the United States for his signature; if he approves he notifies the originating House and sends it to the Secretary of State for publication; if he vetoes he returns the bill with a statement of reasons unless that body has adjourned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also explains concurrent resolutions—though having the effect of law in some respects—are not presented to the President and are generally not used to incorporate legislative matter; their usual uses are for ordering publication and paying expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional use of special commissions and joint investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress frequently makes use of special committees of investigation or joint commissions (examples: industrial commission of 1898; joint commission on immigration of 1907) composed of members of both houses and presidential appointees to investigate subjects and report desirable legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These commissions may be generously funded, establish headquarters, employ investigators, and conduct extensive inquiries (including international research); they often produce voluminous testimony and legislative proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization of executive inquiries and judicial assistance for investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may, by joint resolution, authorize executive officers to conduct inquiries (e.g., instruct the Interstate Commerce Commission to examine railroad discriminations) and may require federal courts to compel witnesses to testify before such commissions; the Supreme Court has upheld such laws as constitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, the Court has limited Congressional authority to impose fines or imprisonment to compel obedience except under the judicial process—i.e., punishment must be imposed by a competent judicial tribunal with jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of Congressional inquiry into executive departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Both houses have long precedents of investigating executive business (sending for persons and papers, examining appropriations application); however, it remains an open question how far Congress may compel executive branches to yield information—examples include a 1909 Senate demand to the Attorney General and the President's directive not to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presidential position cited: department heads are subject to the Constitution and laws but to the direction of the President and to no other direction; thus conflicts may arise between congressional investigatory demands and executive control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee resources and hearing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Each important standing committee has a commodious room, a library of materials, access to Congressional Library resources, stenographic assistance, and often well-paid experts; committees may hold secret sessions admitting only invited persons or open sessions admitting the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness of investigations/hearings depends largely on the skill with which hearings are conducted and the actual interest of committee members in obtaining results; ways and means committee historically holds open sessions and generously allots time before tariff enactments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of floor debate as source of information
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Senate, speeches (particularly on constitutional law) sometimes illuminate problems before the body; in the House debates are often desultory and partisan and do not usually afford much information because the center of gravity has shifted from the House to the committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes Mr. Bryce attributing the absence of informing debates to the committee system and notes the average Representative's tendency to rely on committee reports rather than critically analyze other committees' conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional foundation and congressional power over the judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution vests judicial power in one Supreme Court and in such inferior courts as Congress may from time to time ordain and establish; it is within Congress's power to determine the number of Supreme Court judges and to create additional tribunals deemed necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Constitution seeks to secure judicial independence (judges hold during good behavior and compensation not diminished), federal courts are largely creations of the legislature and Congress can reorganize courts (including past examples of abolishing courts) and thereby affect the judiciary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence protections and congressional levers
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges of Supreme and inferior courts hold office during good behavior and receive compensation not to be diminished while in office; however, Congress may abolish inferior courts, reduce the number of judges by not filling vacancies, or increase the number to influence appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text discusses that Congress cannot remove judges except by impeachment nor abolish the Supreme Court, but it has political methods (e.g., changing court sizes, abolition of positions) that could influence the judiciary; overall the judiciary enjoys, for practical purposes, a high degree of independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment and tenure of federal judges
rubrics_metrics.description: All federal judges are nominated by the President and appointed by and with the advice and consent of the Senate; judges of Supreme and inferior courts hold office during good behavior and therefore cannot be removed except by impeachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Constitution authorizes Congress to vest appointment of some inferior officers in the President alone or other authorities, uniform practice treats judges of inferior federal courts as Presidential nominations with Senate confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court composition, decision-making, and published opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court is composed of nine judges (a Chief Justice and eight Associate Justices); cases are presented by oral argument or printed briefs; each Justice examines facts and arguments independently, conference is held, the Chief Justice requests a colleague to prepare 'the opinion of the court' representing the majority's conclusions, and concurring and dissenting opinions may be prepared; opinions are published as the United States Reports and form the authoritative source on constitutional law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes procedural details (six Judges must be present for decision; majority necessary), the practice of concurring and dissenting opinions, and the importance of opinions in establishing constitutional doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit Courts of Appeals structure and jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediately under the Supreme Court is a Circuit Court of Appeals in each of the nine great circuits; the act of 1891 established these courts to relieve the Supreme Court, and the 1911 statute provided for separate circuit judges; number of judges per circuit varies by business volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuit Courts of Appeals review decisions of lower District Courts, have final decision in many cases (diversity jurisdiction, patent, revenue, criminal), may request instructions from the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court may call cases up or review by certiorari; some cases (constitutional questions, treaties, acts of a state) may be taken directly to the Supreme Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: District Courts organization, terms, and jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The District Court is the lowest federal court; the country is divided into some eighty or ninety districts with one to four district judges appointed by the President and Senate according to business volume; large districts are divided into divisions with statutory dates and places for court terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District Courts try a vast variety of matters; the determination of proper federal forum and the court's jurisdictional scope is a specialized matter generally pursued by practicing lawyers.
